newsitem.title: GERMANY: Grain seen gaining share from imported feeds in EU.
newsitem.headline: Grain seen gaining share from imported feeds in EU.

text.p: European feed grains will continue to gain domestic market share at the expense of imported feeds, Hamburg grain and feeds trade association president Stefan Cremer said on Tuesday.
While overal EU feedstuff demand was rising, especially in Germany, France and Britain, the relative share of imported protein and starch feeds was falling, he said.
Cremer, managing director of Peter Cremer GmbH, was addressing some 400 delegates at an annual trade meeting which followed informal trade consultations.
Grain use in coumpound feed in the EU averaged 44 percent last year, with 35 percent recorded in Germany, he said. The rate was set to rise in 1997.
Compound feed output in the EU in 1997 should be steady or above the 121 million tonnes estimated for 1996.
Feeds imports by the EU in 1996 dropped by three million tonnes to 37 million.
Cremer said he envisaged some two or three million tonnes in additional EU grain export licences in the 1996/97 season, to add to nearly 25 million granted by April 10.
The EU in 1995/96 exported 18 million tonnes.
The industry was concerned the European Commission was planning to present tough rules for the compulsory labelling of gene-modified animal feedstuffs, Cremer said.
A plan backed by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler envisaged labelling all animal feed irrespective of the percentage of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) it contained.
Cremer said Brussels and Bonn authorities should consult the industry before introducing such sweeping changes.
The association also opposed EU Commission plans to sharply cut permissible lead and cadmium content in grain, Cremer said.
There was no proof the levels sought by the Commission were necessary for health reasons. If they were applied, large domestic grain volumes would no longer be marketable.
